name: lsdefine/GenericAgent
methodology_note: Repo-surface track: this product is distributed as a repository (library/CLI) with no web product surface, so the score derives ONLY from measurable public-repository signals — documentation, licensing, maintenance activity, releases, traction, agent-consumability. Each checklist item carries its evidence. Score ceiling 82/100: VITAL requires hands-on behavioral testing that repo signals cannot provide. Replaces a 2026-06/07 stub that carried a default score with no evidence.

hlido_opinion.headline: High-traction self-evolving agent with a genuinely active repo — but the score is repo-signal-only, not a behavioral verdict.
hlido_opinion.body: GenericAgent is one of the higher-traction long-tail repositories in the register: 13.4K GitHub stars, an MIT licence, a README substantial enough (33K chars) to actually onboard from, tagged releases (desktop-portable builds), a CI workflow, and commits landing daily. Its pitch — a self-evolving agent that grows a skill tree from a small seed and claims markedly lower token consumption — is exactly the kind of autonomy claim that only hands-on behavioral testing can confirm, and this review did not run that test. What we can stand behind is the repository hygiene: it is reachable, documented, licensed, maintained, adopted, and carries a CLI install line, so an agent or developer can consume it today. Treat the 82 as a measure of a healthy, agent-consumable open-source project, not a verdict on whether the self-evolution claim holds up in production.

tier_rationale: STEADY (82) is the honest ceiling of the repo-surface track: every measurable public-repository signal is green — reachable, MIT-licensed, 33K-char README, tagged releases, daily commits, a CI workflow, 13.4K stars, documented CLI install. It is not VITAL because VITAL requires hands-on behavioral testing of the self-evolution and token-efficiency claims, which repo signals alone cannot provide.
what_it_does_well: Strong community traction for a long-tail project (13.4K GitHub stars)
Permissive MIT licence — safe to adopt and fork
Substantial README (33K chars) with a documented install/usage path
Actively maintained — commits landing daily at review time
Tagged releases (desktop-portable builds) and a CI workflow present
what_it_fails_at: The headline self-evolution and 6x-token-efficiency claims are unverified — no hands-on behavioral test was run
No web product surface; evaluation is bounded to what the repository exposes
Autonomy that claims 'full system control' warrants sandboxing scrutiny the repo signals cannot assess
best_for: Developers comfortable running and evaluating an autonomous agent from source
Teams wanting an MIT-licensed, CLI-consumable agent base to build on
Anyone tracking the self-evolving / skill-tree agent design space
not_recommended_for: Buyers needing a vendor-supported, behaviorally-benchmarked product
Environments where an agent claiming 'full system control' cannot be safely sandboxed
Non-technical users — there is no hosted product surface

compared_to.verdict_diff: Langroid is a mature multi-agent programming framework with a broader contributor base; GenericAgent is a single self-evolving-agent bet. Choose Langroid to build multi-agent systems; choose GenericAgent to study or extend the self-evolution approach.
